title: US Takes 35% Stake in Venezuela's 65-Billion-Barrel Oil Deal via Pentagon Office; Hormuz Hostilities Resume as Two Saudi Tankers Struck
subhead: Washington formalized a sweeping Venezuela oil arrangement — 17 fields, 100-year concessions, a Pentagon equity stake — while renewed US-Iran strikes and tanker attacks near Hormuz pushed Brent above $92 and European gas to six-month highs.

sections.heading: The Venezuela Deal: Pentagon Equity, 100-Year Concessions, 65 Billion Barrels
sections.body:
The White House released a fact sheet on Aug. 31 detailing the US-Venezuela oil agreement President Trump first announced on Aug. 28. Venezuelan interim authorities granted North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), the firm of businessman Alejandro Betancourt López, 100-year concessions covering 17 oil fields with roughly 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, according to the fact sheet and World Oil. NABEP plans to invest up to $100 billion in Venezuelan infrastructure to lift production from inactive or underperforming fields.

The unusual structure is the story. The Pentagon's little-known Office of Strategic Capital — created in 2022 to bolster defense industrial production and now run under Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg — will take a 35% equity stake in NABEP's corporate parent via penny warrants, plus veto authority over board appointments, the Philadelphia Inquirer reports. The State Department gets the right to buy 20% of production at cost and a right of first refusal on the remaining 80%, which the White House says could feed the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The administration frames the deal as 'at zero cost to the United States.'

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright traveled to Caracas and said Tuesday that deals signed there would lead to Venezuelan output more than doubling in the next few years, per Reuters. Separately, Bloomberg reported Sept. 1 that Chevron — the only US major currently operating in Venezuela — is nearing an agreement for operating rights to two large Orinoco Belt fields.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a new model of US energy statecraft: a defense-investment office taking equity in a foreign oil venture to secure offtake, rather than sanctions or traditional diplomacy. It also signals Washington actively courting Venezuela's reserves as a hedge against Hormuz disruption — and China has already demanded guarantees for its own interests in the country.

sections.heading: Hormuz Hostilities Resume: Two Saudi Tankers Struck, US Hits IRGC Targets
sections.body:
The month-long lull in the US-Iran war broke Monday. Two oil supertankers exiting the Strait of Hormuz were struck by projectiles, maritime security firm Marisks reported: the Sidr, a very large crude carrier operated by Saudi Arabia's Bahri, hit northeast of Khasab, Oman, and the Senegal Prosperity, operated by South Korea's Sinokor Group, struck by three projectiles east of Oman, per Bloomberg/World Oil. Both were sailing dark with AIS transponders off. No group claimed responsibility.

The US said it targeted Iranian rocket launchers preparing to lay mines in the strait; Iran retaliated with missile and drone attacks on the UAE and Jordan, with no reported damage. On Tuesday, CENTCOM confirmed renewed strikes on IRGC targets in Iran, and Trump said the strikes were ongoing, per The Nation and Greek Reporter. A senior US official told Channel 12 the US is now applying a new 'tanker-for-tanker' policy — striking an Iranian state oil tanker each time Tehran hits a tanker in the strait. Brent crude rose about 1.7% to above $92 a barrel on the renewed fighting.

Oil shipments through Hormuz had recovered to roughly half of pre-war levels during the lull, aided by clandestine shuttle runs, with Aramco resuming loadings from Ras Tanura and offering cargoes from the Gulf of Oman after months of diverting to Red Sea ports.
sections.whyItMatters: The recovery in Hormuz flows — the key reason oil had eased — is now at risk of reversing. The new tanker-for-tanker policy directly targets Iran's oil export revenue, escalating the economic dimension of the conflict even as the military exchanges resume.

sections.heading: QatarEnergy Extends LNG Force Majeure; European Gas Hits Six-Month High
sections.body:
QatarEnergy has again extended force majeure on LNG deliveries to Europe and Asia as regular shipping through Hormuz remains largely halted, Euronews reports. Italian utility Edison said QatarEnergy will miss another five cargoes scheduled between late September and early November, bringing affected cargoes under its contract to 29 since April — about 3.8 billion cubic metres. Qatar has told buyers in Pakistan cancellations will continue into October, and supplies to Bangladesh remain affected beyond September.

The disruption has removed most Qatari LNG from the global market: Qatar exported only 18 cargoes in the first six months of the war versus 509 a year earlier, per ICIS data, costing an estimated $24 billion in lost sales. Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy scholar Anne-Sophie Corbeau said QatarEnergy is renewing force majeure month by month because it still has no reliable date for resumption. Replacement supply from the US, Canada, Nigeria and Malaysia has not covered the full shortfall. European gas prices climbed to their highest level since March on Tuesday as renewed US-Iran exchanges raised LNG supply concerns, and Asian spot LNG hit a five-month high, per Bloomberg.
sections.whyItMatters: Qatar's prolonged absence from the LNG market is the quiet structural driver of high gas prices on both sides of the world. With Hormuz flows again under threat, buyers face a winter where the single largest LNG supplier remains effectively offline.

sections.heading: Russia Doubles Its LNG Dark Fleet as Arctic LNG 2 Ramps for China
sections.body:
Russia has nearly doubled the fleet of tankers serving its US-sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project in under a year, from 11 ships at the end of December to at least 20, according to a Bloomberg analysis of ship-tracking data. The latest addition is a Russian-built ice-class vessel, the second designed to traverse icy waters year-round, tracked picking up a shipment over the weekend. Most of the fleet has the opaque ownership typical of dark-fleet vessels.

The catch, Bloomberg notes, is that China is effectively the only buyer of the sanctioned LNG. The Trump administration has not taken a hard line against Russia's gas industry or the growing dark fleet, and has not restricted China's purchases of the blacklisted fuel — a contrast with the Biden administration's sanctions on Arctic LNG 2 and its supporting vessels. The Arctic Institute's Malte Humpert said Moscow is 'putting in place the logistics to deliver increasing amounts of LNG to Asia.'
sections.whyItMatters: Russia is quietly rebuilding its gas export machine around a single sanctioned project and a single buyer, with Washington declining to enforce the previous administration's restrictions. The dark-fleet build-out is a direct test of whether US sanctions on Russian energy still bite.

sections.heading: SCO Summit: Xi-Putin Gas Talks and a Multipolar Energy Bloc
sections.body:
At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met Monday to discuss bilateral relations including, per the Russian side, gas — keeping the long-stalled Power of Siberia 2 pipeline on the agenda, Bloomberg and Pipeline Journal report. Beijing's foreign ministry said China is 'ready to work with Russia to continuously deepen practical bilateral cooperation.' The summit also saw Putin reaffirm Moscow's alliance with Iran's President Masud Pezeshkian amid the US-Iran war, per RFE/RL, and the SCO issued statements slamming attacks and sanctions on Iran.

The SCO, which accounts for about 43% of the world's population and 23% of global GDP, framed itself as a multipolar counterweight to Western-led institutions, per Yahoo News and OilPrice. The energy dimension is central: Russia's gas pivot east, Iran's position as a sanctioned producer, and China's demand all converge in this bloc.
sections.whyItMatters: The SCO is consolidating as an energy-aligned bloc of sanctioned and non-Western producers. Power of Siberia 2 remains stalled on price, but the political scaffolding around a Russia-China-Iran energy axis is being reinforced at a moment when Hormuz disruption raises the value of overland alternatives.

bottomLine: Two forces moved energy markets today. Washington formalized an unprecedented Venezuela arrangement — a Pentagon investment office taking a 35% equity stake in a 65-billion-barrel venture with 100-year concessions — signaling the US is building a non-Hormuz supply hedge through direct state equity rather than sanctions. Simultaneously, the US-Iran war resumed in earnest: two Saudi tankers were struck near Hormuz, CENTCOM confirmed strikes on IRGC targets, and a new tanker-for-tanker policy targets Iran's oil revenue. Brent pushed above $92, European gas hit six-month highs, and QatarEnergy's LNG force majeure — now in its sixth month — keeps the world's largest LNG supplier offline. The Venezuela deal is a long-term hedge; the Hormuz escalation is the immediate risk.
sources: World Oil, Philadelphia Inquirer, Reuters, Bloomberg, The Nation, Greek Reporter, Euronews, Columbia Center on Global Energy Policy, ICIS, gCaptain, RFE/RL, Yahoo News, OilPrice, Pipeline Journal, TASS
